opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it's less about a formal org chart and more about recognizing what each of us was already doing before the company existed. The four of us have worked together on the open-source project for years, so by the time we started the company we already had a very clear sense of each other's strengths. The division mostly just made explicit what had naturally emerged.

Roughly speaking, one person leans toward the business side: talking to customers, fundraising, building the team, being the external face of the company. Someone else is the deep systems person, closest to the core engine architecture and the hard performance problems. Another focuses on research direction, thinking about where models and hardware are heading in two or three years so we aren't just reacting. My own role sits close to the community and the infrastructure that connects everything: hardware vendor integrations, the plugin and distributed pieces, and making sure the open-source project stays healthy as it grows. For a project like ours, the community is the product in a sense, so that can't be an afterthought.

But I'd stress that the boundaries are pretty soft. We're still a small, very technical team, and all four of us write code and review PRs. When there's a big release or a new model launch where we need day-zero support, everyone jumps in regardless of title.

The principle I care about most is that each area needs one clear owner who makes the final call. Four smart, opinionated engineers can debate forever otherwise. So we discuss openly, and then the person who owns that domain decides, and the rest of us commit. That trust comes from years of working together before there was any money or equity involved, and I think that history is honestly our biggest advantage as a founding team.

r001.rationale: The response says roles reflect each founder’s prior work and strengths, and that each domain has a clear owner. It does not clearly state that responsibilities are allocated according to who has the most relevant context for a given task.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I don't think of it as "dividing" so much as letting the division emerge from what each of us can't help doing anyway.

When the four of us started, we didn't sit down with a whiteboard and assign titles. We'd already worked together for a long time in the open-source community, so we each had a very clear sense of where the others were strongest and, maybe more importantly, where they'd get bored or frustrated. That's actually the most useful information for a founding team. You can learn skills, but you can't fake caring about something for years.

So the rough shape is this. One of us is naturally the person who thinks about where the whole field is going in three years, and whether what we're building still matters then. That's the product and direction role, even if we don't call it that. One of us is the person who, if you give them a system that's "working," will immediately go find the three things that are quietly wrong with it. That's the engineering backbone. One of us is the person everybody outside the company wants to talk to, because they explain things well and they're patient with people who aren't deep in the weeds. That ends up covering users, community, hiring, and a lot of the external relationship side. And then one of us is the person who makes sure the trains run on time, that we actually ship instead of endlessly polishing, and that nobody's quietly drowning in work.

My own role is mostly on the systems and infrastructure side, which is where I've spent most of my career. But I'd say the honest answer is that in a four-person founding team, everyone does everything at least some of the time. I've written docs, I've done interviews, I've argued with cloud providers. The "division" is really about who has the final say when there's a disagreement in a particular area, not about who's allowed to touch what.

The thing I'd caution against, and this comes from watching other teams, is dividing too cleanly too early. If you carve up the company into four kingdoms on day one, you get four people optimizing for their own kingdom. What you actually want is four people who all feel responsible for the whole thing but trust each other enough to defer. That trust is the hard part. Org charts are easy.

r001.rationale: The response says roles emerged from each founder’s strengths and interests, and that people defer in their areas. It does not state that responsibilities are allocated according to who has the most relevant context for a task.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to make ownership clear without making the boundaries too rigid. With four founders, you want each person to own an area where they can contribute the most and have the authority to make decisions there. Otherwise, everyone ends up discussing everything, and progress gets slow.

At the same time, the major decisions—what we’re building, who we’re serving, and where the company is going—need to be shared. So I’d distinguish between having a voice and owning the final decision. We should be able to challenge one another, but we also need to trust the person responsible for carrying the work forward. And that division should evolve as the company grows.

r001.rationale: The response assigns areas based on where each founder can contribute most, but does not say responsibility should go to whoever has the most relevant context for the task.

sol-6.1.text: I think the key is to make responsibilities clear without turning them into rigid boundaries. Each of the four founders should own an area where they’re strongest and be accountable for the decisions there. For decisions that affect the whole company, we need to discuss them together, but we shouldn’t require all four people to approve every detail. And as the company grows, we should be willing to adjust that division.
